props.title: The Best Man
props.initialSlug: Political rivals battle for presidential nomination

sections.content: The Best Man represents one of the sharpest political dramas ever made, adapting Gore Vidal's stage play into a prescient examination of presidential politics. The film pits Henry Fonda's principled intellectual William Russell against Cliff Robertson's opportunistic Joe Cantwell in a bitter convention fight for their party's nomination. It shares DNA with later political classics like All the President's Men (1976) and The Candidate (1972), but its exploration of character assassination and moral compromise feels ripped from today's headlines.

sections.content: The 1960s marked a turning point for political films, moving away from rah-rah patriotism toward more cynical examinations of power. Dr. Strangelove (1964) used dark comedy to expose nuclear madness, while Fail Safe (1964) approached similar material with dead-serious intensity. The Best Man fits perfectly in this era, using backroom dealing and character assassination to show how the sausage of presidential politics gets made.

Gore Vidal's screenplay crackles with memorable dialogue and complex moral situations that echo through later films like Primary Colors (1998) and Bulworth (1998). The central conflict between Fonda's intellectual liberal and Robertson's ruthless conservative created a template for exploring political polarization that remains relevant, seen in films like Ides of March (2011) and Long Shot (2019). sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond obvious political thrillers. Its DNA can be found in everything from Aaron Sorkin's work in The American President (1995) to the cynical power plays of House of Cards (2013-2018). The way it handles political conventions and behind-the-scenes machinations influenced films like Game Change (2012) and Recount (2008), showing how the political process really works.
